# ui.R
# Mobile-first bottom-nav layout, built directly with shiny::tags/htmltools so
# the visual result matches the original vanilla-JS app (css ported to
# www/style.css) rather than adopting a generic Shiny theme.

# TECHNIQUE_CHOICES lives in global.R (shared with server.R -- ui.R and
# server.R are sourced into sibling environments, only global.R is common).

nav_button <- function(id, icon, label) {
  actionButton(id, label = tagList(span(class = "navicon", icon, "aria-hidden" = "true"), span(label)),
               class = "navbtn")
}

#' Minimal inline-SVG line icons (stroke = currentColor, so each inherits
#' the nav button's own text colour, including its active-state colour
#' change, with no separate CSS needed per icon). Deliberately hand-drawn
#' shapes, not a Font Awesome/icon-font dependency: this app has to work
#' fully offline/embedded (Moodle iframe, no guaranteed network), and an
#' icon font or CDN reference would silently fail or block in exactly the
#' contexts this app is built for.
nav_icon_svg <- function(path_content) {
  HTML(sprintf(
    '<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="20" height="20" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round">%s</svg>',
    path_content
  ))
}
ICON_DATA     <- nav_icon_svg('<rect x="3" y="4" width="18" height="16" rx="2"/><line x1="3" y1="10" x2="21" y2="10"/><line x1="9" y1="10" x2="9" y2="20"/><line x1="15" y1="10" x2="15" y2="20"/>')
ICON_ANALYSE  <- nav_icon_svg('<line x1="4" y1="20" x2="4" y2="12"/><line x1="10" y1="20" x2="10" y2="6"/><line x1="16" y1="20" x2="16" y2="14"/><line x1="20" y1="20" x2="20" y2="9"/><line x1="2" y1="20" x2="22" y2="20"/>')
ICON_RESULTS  <- nav_icon_svg('<path d="M14 3H6a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v14a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h12a2 2 0 0 0 2-2V9z"/><path d="M14 3v6h6"/><line x1="8" y1="13" x2="16" y2="13"/><line x1="8" y1="17" x2="13" y2="17"/>')
ICON_LEARN    <- nav_icon_svg('<path d="M2 5.5C2 4.7 2.7 4 3.5 4H10a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v14a2 2 0 0 0-2-2H3.5A1.5 1.5 0 0 1 2 16.5z"/><path d="M22 5.5c0-.8-.7-1.5-1.5-1.5H14a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v14a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h6.5a1.5 1.5 0 0 0 1.5-1.5z"/>')

ui <- fluidPage(
  # fluidPage (not tagList) so Shiny's Bootstrap JS loads -- tabsetPanel's
  # show/hide switching depends on Bootstrap's jQuery .tab() plugin, which a
  # bare tagList never loads. Our own www/style.css still loads after
  # Bootstrap's and takes precedence for every class it defines.
  title = APP_NAME,
  tags$head(
    tags$meta(charset = "UTF-8"),
    tags$meta(name = "viewport", content = "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, viewport-fit=cover"),
    tags$title(APP_NAME),
    tags$link(rel = "stylesheet", href = "style.css")
  ),
  tags$div(id = "app",
    tags$header(class = "topbar",
      tags$div(class = "topbar-title",
        tags$span(class = "brand-mark", APP_NAME),
        tags$span(class = "subtitle", "Statistics, in your browser")
      )
    ),
    tags$main(id = "panels",
      tabsetPanel(id = "tabs", type = "hidden",

        tabPanelBody("panel-data",
          tags$h1("Data"),
          tags$p(class = "lede", "Load a demo dataset, or bring in your own CSV file. Nothing leaves this device, R runs directly in your browser."),

          tags$div(class = "two-col-row",
            tags$div(class = "card",
              tags$h2("Show"),
              tags$div(class = "filter-toggle-row",
                checkboxInput("show_demo", "Demo", value = TRUE),
                checkboxInput("show_lecture", "Lecture", value = TRUE),
                checkboxInput("show_tutorial", "Tutorial", value = TRUE),
                checkboxInput("show_selflearn", "Self-learning", value = TRUE),
                checkboxInput("show_upload", "Upload data", value = TRUE)
              )
            ),
            # Column radio list, not a dropdown -- with 47 demos the picker
            # needs a filter that narrows the list before it renders, not a
            # single long scroll. radioButtons() stacks vertically by
            # default (no inline = TRUE), which is the "column" layout.
            # No "All" choice: nothing selected (selected = character(0))
            # means unfiltered, same result, one fewer row on a screen
            # already long enough on mobile. Only shown while Demo itself
            # is toggled on -- picking a technique is meaningless once the
            # demo list it filters is hidden.
            conditionalPanel(condition = "input.show_demo",
              tags$div(class = "card",
                tags$h2("Technique"),
                radioButtons("demo_technique", NULL, choices = TECHNIQUE_CHOICES, selected = character(0))
              )
            )
          ),
          uiOutput("data_library_box"),
          uiOutput("upload_box"),

          uiOutput("data_summary_box"),
          uiOutput("variables_box"),
          uiOutput("cleaning_box"),
          uiOutput("data_grid_box")
        ),

        tabPanelBody("panel-analyse",
          tags$h1("Analyse"),
          tags$p(class = "lede", "Choose a technique. Each one checks its data requirements before it runs."),
          uiOutput("no_data_warning"),
          uiOutput("analysis_picker")
        ),

        tabPanelBody("panel-results",
          tags$h1("Results"),
          uiOutput("results_body"),
          uiOutput("writeup_block"),
          uiOutput("interpretation_block"),
          uiOutput("report_block"),
          uiOutput("history_block")
        ),

        tabPanelBody("panel-learn",
          tags$h1("Learn"),
          tags$p(class = "lede", "Short, plain explanations of each technique."),
          uiOutput("learn_body")
        )
      )
    ),
    tags$nav(class = "bottomnav", `aria-label` = "Sections",
      nav_button("nav_data", ICON_DATA, "Data"),
      nav_button("nav_analyse", ICON_ANALYSE, "Analyse"),
      nav_button("nav_results", ICON_RESULTS, "Results"),
      nav_button("nav_learn", ICON_LEARN, "Learn")
    )
  )
)

name: global.R
content:
# global.R
# Shared, pure-R analysis functions for PocketStat (shinylive build). A
# general-purpose in-browser statistics tool, not tied to any one course or
# module -- no course-specific branding or references belong in this file.
#
# Every statistical computation here is either a base R function (t.test, aov,
# chisq.test, cor.test, lm, factanal, TukeyHSD, kruskal.test, shapiro.test) or
# one of the two textbook-formula exceptions below (Levene's/Brown-Forsythe,
# Cronbach's alpha), base R has no built-in for either. No custom
# reimplementation of a standard test. No MCDM/decision-analysis content.
#
# Every run_*() has a matching plot_*(). Every run_*() returns:
#   list(main = data.frame, assumptions = data.frame | NULL,
#        effect_size = data.frame | NULL, note = character | NULL,
#        code = character)

library(shiny)
library(rhandsontable)
library(htmltools)

# Shared between ui.R and server.R -- must live here, not in ui.R, because
# Shiny sources ui.R/server.R into sibling environments; only global.R's
# bindings are visible to both.
APP_NAME <- "PocketStat"

TECHNIQUE_CHOICES <- c(
  "Descriptive statistics"         = "descriptive",
  "Distribution shape"             = "distribution",
  "Z-scores & empirical rule"      = "zscore",
  "One-sample test"                = "onesample",
  "Two-sample test"                = "twosample",
  "One-way ANOVA"                  = "oneway",
  "Kruskal-Wallis"                 = "kruskal",
  "Correlation"                    = "correlation",
  "Correlation matrix"             = "cormatrix",
  "Chi-squared"                    = "chisquare",
  "Simple linear regression"       = "regression",
  "Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)" = "reliability",
  "Factor analysis (EFA)"          = "factoranalysis"
)

#' Curated demo datasets, one well-matched dataset per technique (the
#' JASP/jamovi Data Library pattern -- a single stretched-thin sample
#' dataset is not a good demo for every technique).
#'
#' Simulated business data, not real-world textbook datasets. An earlier
#' version of this list used base R's own `datasets` package (chick feed
#' weights, river lengths, sleeping-pill trials, car stopping distances) --
#' real, verifiable, well-known, and a genuine mismatch for a tool meant to
#' support teaching business decision-making. A real dataset from an
#' unrelated domain is not a better demo than a simulated one from the
#' right domain; relevance to what is actually being taught matters more
#' than the data being literally real. Every dataset below is generated
#' with a fixed seed (`set.seed(2026)`, see the generation script noted in
#' CLAUDE.md) so it is exactly reproducible, and every number in
#' `interpretation` is the real output of running this app's own
#' `run_*()` functions against that generated data (see tests/test-cases.md
#' for the verification run) -- simulated inputs, never a fabricated
#' result on top of them.
#'
#' `interpretation` is written as a Result (APA-style: t/F/r/chi-squared/
#' R-squared with df, exact p where reasonable) followed by an Implication
#' (what the result means for a manager, then what it suggests doing or
#' watching for). Where a result came back non-significant or otherwise
#' not the "clean" outcome a tidier simulation could have produced (see
#' `pilot_campaign`), that is reported honestly rather than re-seeded
#' until it looked better -- a small pilot failing to reach significance
#' is itself a real and common business lesson, not a demo to hide.
#'
#' `context` tags which of the Data tab's show/hide filters a demo appears
#' under. Every entry here is "demo" only -- self-learning content is
#' separate material, not this dataset library, so nothing is tagged
#' "self_learning" (a prior version double-tagged everything, since
#' reverted). No entry is tagged "lecture" or "tutorial" yet either: that
#' would need content actually designed for a live-taught session or a
#' structured hands-on worksheet, which none of these are, tagging them so
#' would overstate what exists.
EXAMPLE_DATASETS <- list(
  list(id = "store_revenue", title = "Monthly revenue by store format", technique = "descriptive",
       file = "examples/store_revenue.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "40 stores' monthly revenue (GBP '000s) and format (Flagship/Standard/Express). One scale and one nominal variable.",
       interpretation = "Result: mean monthly revenue was GBP 454.5k (SD = 71.0, n = 40); format was mostly Standard (28 stores, 70%), with fewer Express (10, 25%) and Flagship (2, 5%) sites. Implication: an SD of GBP 71k on a GBP 454.5k mean implies real store-to-store variation even within the same estate, which further suggests a head office comparing branches against the network average should check format mix first, since the small Flagship sample here would make any single Flagship store look like an outlier by pure chance."),
  list(id = "complaint_resolution", title = "Customer complaint resolution time", technique = "distribution",
       file = "examples/complaint_resolution.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "60 customer service complaints, hours to resolution. Right-skewed, most complaints close quickly, a few drag on.",
       interpretation = "Result: skewness = 0.74, Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.94, p = .007, rejecting normality. Implication: the right skew implies most complaints are resolved quickly while a minority take much longer and pull the average up, which further suggests a customer service team should report the median resolution time in its SLA dashboard, not the mean, or a handful of difficult cases will make ordinary performance look worse than it is."),
  list(id = "production_output", title = "Daily production line output", technique = "zscore",
       file = "examples/production_output.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "60 days of units produced on a manufacturing line. Roughly normal, good for checking the empirical rule against real-looking operational data.",
       interpretation = "Result: mean daily output was 499.7 units (SD = 22.9); 65.0% of days fell within 1 SD of the mean, 95.0% within 2 SD, 100% within 3 SD, close to the empirical rule's 68/95/99.7 expectation. Implication: this closeness implies day-to-day output variation is ordinary common-cause variation, not a sign of a process problem, which further suggests a plant manager could reasonably use the empirical rule itself to set a simple early-warning band (for example, flag any day beyond 2 SD) without needing a more complex quality-control model."),
  list(id = "call_duration", title = "Call-centre handling time vs SLA", technique = "onesample",
       file = "examples/call_duration.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "35 customer service calls, minutes to handle. Tests the average against a 6-minute service-level benchmark.",
       interpretation = "Result: mean call handling time was 6.65 minutes, one-sample t(34) = 2.72, p = .010, against a 6-minute SLA benchmark, Cohen's d = 0.46 (small). Implication: this implies the team is reliably running over its own benchmark on average, not just on a few unlucky calls, which further suggests management should investigate a process cause (call scripts, staffing at peak times) before setting a stricter target, since a small but real gap like this usually needs a process fix, not just a reminder to agents to talk faster."),
  list(id = "store_sales", title = "Weekly sales, Store A vs Store B", technique = "twosample",
       file = "examples/store_sales.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "48 weekly sales figures (GBP '000s), 24 from each of two stores. Independent samples, pick the Independent samples t-test option.",
       interpretation = "Result: Store A averaged GBP 60.5k a week versus Store B's GBP 48.0k, independent-samples t(45.7) = 5.34, p < .001, Cohen's d = 1.54 (large). Implication: this implies a real, sizeable performance gap between the two stores rather than normal week-to-week noise, which further suggests management should investigate what Store A is doing differently (footfall, staffing, local competition) before assuming Store B's team is simply underperforming, since the cause could just as easily be location or catchment."),
  list(id = "training_productivity", title = "Employee productivity before/after training", technique = "twosample",
       file = "examples/training_productivity.csv", context = c("demo"),
       description = "18 employees' productivity scores measured before and after a training programme, paired design (row order matches employee to employee). Pick the Paired t-test option.",
       interpretation = "Result: mean productivity rose from 71.7 before training to 79.4 after, paired t(17) = 9.04, p < .001, Cohen's d = 2.13 (large). Implication: this implies the training programme is associated with a substantial, consistent improvement for these same employees, which further suggests it is worth rolling out more widely, while remembering that a before/after design without a control group cannot fully separate the training's effect from other things that changed over the same period."),
  list(id = "regional_satisfaction", title = "Customer satisfaction across regional offices", technique = "oneway",
       file = "examples/regional_satisfaction.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "48 customer satisfaction scores (1-10) across three regional offices (North/South/East). The standard one-way ANOVA setup.",
       interpretation = "Result: satisfaction differed across the three regions, F(2, 45) = 8.09, p = .001, eta-squared = .26. Implication: this implies at least one region is genuinely out of line with the others rather than the difference being down to chance, which further suggests running the Tukey HSD follow-up (in the R code output) to identify which specific region needs attention before deciding where to invest in a service-improvement programme."),
  list(id = "support_tickets", title = "Support ticket resolution time by tier", technique = "kruskal",
       file = "examples/support_tickets.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "54 support tickets, hours to resolution, across three support tiers. Skewed, a realistic case for the non-parametric alternative to ANOVA.",
       interpretation = "Result: resolution time differed across the three tiers, Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared(2) = 22.65, p < .001. Implication: this implies the tiers are not performing equivalently, which further suggests using resolution-time-by-tier as a genuine capacity-planning input, for example staffing the slower tier more heavily, rather than assuming ticket complexity alone explains the gap."),
  list(id = "marketing_sales", title = "Marketing spend vs monthly revenue", technique = "correlation",
       file = "examples/marketing_sales.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "32 months of marketing spend and revenue (GBP '000s) for a small retail business. A strong, realistic positive relationship.",
       interpretation = "Result: marketing spend and revenue were strongly positively correlated, r(30) = .90, p < .001, 95% CI [.79, .95]. Implication: this implies months with higher marketing spend tend to be months with higher revenue, which further suggests marketing spend is a reasonable lever to test further (for example via a controlled budget increase), while remembering a strong correlation alone does not prove the spend caused the revenue, seasonal effects could be driving both."),
  list(id = "business_metrics", title = "Marketing spend, revenue, satisfaction, staff count", technique = "cormatrix",
       file = "examples/business_metrics.csv", context = c("demo"),
       description = "The same 32-month business dataset, four variables at once (marketing spend, revenue, customer satisfaction, staff count). Shows a correlation matrix rather than one pair at a time.",
       interpretation = "Result: marketing spend correlated strongly with both revenue (r = .90) and satisfaction (r = .68), but staff count was unrelated to any of the other three (r's from -.12 to .04, all ns). Implication: this implies marketing spend, revenue, and satisfaction move together as one cluster while staffing levels tell a genuinely separate story, which further suggests a manager should not expect adding staff alone to move revenue or satisfaction in this business, whatever is driving those three appears to sit elsewhere."),
  list(id = "channel_loyalty", title = "Purchase channel by loyalty tier", technique = "chisquare",
       file = "examples/channel_loyalty.csv", context = c("demo"),
 description = "150 customers, purchase channel (Online/In-store) by loyalty tier (Bronze/Silver/Gold). The standard chi-squared test of association.",
       interpretation = "Result: purchase channel and loyalty tier were associated, chi-squared(2, N = 150) = 7.12, p = .028, Cramer's V = .22. Implication: this implies higher-tier customers are not shopping the same way as lower-tier ones, which further suggests a retailer's channel investment (for example online account features versus in-store service) should be matched to which tier actually uses that channel, rather than applying one channel strategy to the whole loyalty base."),
  list(id = "pilot_campaign", title = "Small pilot: campaign response by customer segment", technique = "chisquare",
       file = "examples/pilot_campaign.csv", context = c("demo"),
       description = "A 22-customer pilot campaign, response (Responded/No response) by segment (New/Existing). Small cell counts, needs Fisher's exact test rather than chi-squared.",
       interpretation = "Result: Fisher's exact test found no statistically significant association between segment and response in this pilot, p = .659, odds ratio = 0.47 (95% CI [0.05, 3.59]), despite existing customers responding numerically more often (5 of 11) than new customers (3 of 11). Implication: this implies the apparent gap in this pilot is not strong enough evidence to act on, which further suggests the honest conclusion is \"inconclusive, not proven equal or proven different\": with only 11 customers per segment the pilot is under-powered to detect a real difference of this size, and the right next step is a larger test, not a decision based on the raw percentages alone."),
  list(id = "ad_spend_revenue", title = "Advertising spend predicting revenue", technique = "regression",
       file = "examples/ad_spend_revenue.csv", context = c("demo"),
       description = "The same 32-month marketing dataset, used to predict revenue from advertising spend. The standard simple linear regression setup.",
       interpretation = "Result: revenue = GBP 46.6k + GBP 3.96k per GBP 1k of ad spend, R-squared = .80, p < .001. #' Levene's test (Brown-Forsythe form: deviations from the group MEDIAN).
#' Base R has no built-in equal-variance test; this is the standard textbook
#' formula (one-way ANOVA on absolute deviations from each group's median).
levene_test <- function(y, g) {
  g <- factor(g)
  med <- ave(y, g, FUN = median)
  d <- abs(y - med)
  fit <- aov(d ~ g)
  s <- summary(fit)[[1]]
  data.frame(
    check = "Levene's test (equal variances)",
    statistic = round(s[1, "F value"], 4),
    df = paste(s[1, "Df"], s[2, "Df"], sep = ", "),
    p_value = round(s[1, "Pr(>F)"], 4),
    result = ifelse(s[1, "Pr(>F)"] < 0.05,
                     "Variances differ significantly (p < .05)",
                     "No evidence variances differ (p >= .05)")
  )
}

#' Shapiro-Wilk normality check, returned in the same {check, statistic, ...}
#' shape as levene_test() so assumption tables stack cleanly.
shapiro_row <- function(x, label = "Shapiro-Wilk (normality)") {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) < 3 || length(x) > 5000) {
    return(data.frame(check = label, statistic = NA, df = NA, p_value = NA,
                       result = "Not run (needs 3-5000 observations)"))
  }
  sw <- shapiro.test(x)
  data.frame(
    check = label,
    statistic = round(unname(sw$statistic), 4),
    df = NA,
    p_value = round(sw$p.value, 4),
    result = ifelse(sw$p.value < 0.05,
                     "Departs from normal (p < .05)",
                     "Consistent with normal (p >= .05)")
  )
}

#' Cronbach's alpha. Base R has no built-in; this is the standard formula
#' (k/(k-1)) * (1 - sum(item variances) / variance(total score)).
cronbach_alpha <- function(items) {
  items <- items[stats::complete.cases(items), , drop = FALSE]
  k <- ncol(items)
  total <- rowSums(items)
  item_var_sum <- sum(apply(items, 2, var))
  alpha <- (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - item_var_sum / var(total))
  list(alpha = alpha, total = total, k = k)
}

#' Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy: overall KMO and
#' per-item MSA, from the anti-image correlation matrix (the inverse of
#' the correlation matrix). No base R built-in (confirmed: exists("KMO")
#' is FALSE; the usual source is the psych package, a new webR-wasm
#' dependency this project has deliberately avoided elsewhere), so this is
#' the standard textbook formula, not a novel one, same category as
#' levene_test()/cronbach_alpha() above.
kmo_measure <- function(mat) {
  R <- cor(mat, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  R_inv <- solve(R)
  d <- 1 / sqrt(diag(R_inv))
  partial <- -sweep(sweep(R_inv, 1, d, "*"), 2, d, "*")
  diag(partial) <- 0
  r_off <- R; diag(r_off) <- 0
  sum_r2 <- sum(r_off^2)
  sum_p2 <- sum(partial^2)
  overall <- sum_r2 / (sum_r2 + sum_p2)
  msa <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(R)), function(i) {
    r2_i <- sum(r_off[i, ]^2); p2_i <- sum(partial[i, ]^2)
    r2_i / (r2_i + p2_i)
  }, numeric(1))
  list(overall = overall, msa = stats::setNames(msa, colnames(mat)))
}

#' Bartlett's test of sphericity: is the correlation matrix significantly
#' different from an identity matrix (i.e. is factor analysis worthwhile
#' at all)? No base R built-in -- confirmed stats::bartlett.test() is a
#' different test entirely (homogeneity of variances across groups), reusing
#' it here by name-confusion would be a real correctness bug, not a
#' shortcut. Standard chi-square approximation from the correlation
#' matrix's determinant.
bartlett_sphericity <- function(mat) {
  R <- cor(mat, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  n <- nrow(mat); p <- ncol(R)
  det_r <- det(R)
  chi_sq <- -(n - 1 - (2 * p + 5) / 6) * log(det_r)
  df <- p * (p - 1) / 2
  list(chi_sq = chi_sq, df = df, p_value = 1 - pchisq(chi_sq, df))
}

#' Magnitude label for Cohen's d.
cohend_label <- function(d) {
  ad <- abs(d)
  if (ad < 0.2) "negligible" else if (ad < 0.5) "small"
  else if (ad < 0.8) "medium" else "large"
}

#' Cramer's V for a chi-squared test of association.
cramers_v <- function(chisq, n, r, c) {
  sqrt(unname(chisq) / (n * (min(r, c) - 1)))
}

plot_theme <- function() par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), family = "sans", cex.main = 1, font.main = 2)

#' Wrap a plot title across multiple lines at word boundaries when it's
#' long enough to run off a narrow panel. Confirmed directly: real Label
#' text (e.g. "Monthly revenue (GBP '000s)") is often much longer than
#' the raw column name it replaces, and a plot_batch() 2-up grid panel is
#' roughly half the canvas width -- a title built from a long Label
#' overran the right edge of the image, the same "outside the print area"
#' failure as the rotated-axis-label bug above, just at the top instead
#' of the bottom. Every plot_*() with a var_label()-built title wraps it
#' through this and widens its top margin with title_top_margin() below,
#' to make room for the extra line(s) this can add.
wrap_title <- function(s, width = 34) paste(strwrap(s, width = width), collapse = "\n")

#' Top margin (in lines) wide enough for a title already run through
#' wrap_title() -- one line fits in plot_theme()'s default 3, each
#' wrapped line beyond that needs roughly one more.
title_top_margin <- function(wrapped_title) 2 + length(strsplit(wrapped_title, "\n")[[1]])

#' Bottom margin (in lines) wide enough for rotated (las = 2) category axis
#' labels. plot_theme()'s fixed 4-line bottom margin is sized for short
#' horizontal axis text; rotated labels run downward instead of sideways,
#' and anything longer than a couple of characters gets clipped against the
#' image edge -- confirmed directly against the store_format demo, where
#' "Standard"/"Flagship" were cut off top and bottom. Every barplot() call
#' using las = 2 must widen the bottom margin with this before drawing,
#' the same fix already applied to plot_correlation_matrix()'s left margin
#' for the same reason (long row labels, rotated, past the default margin).
rotated_bottom_margin <- function(labels) max(4, 2 + max(nchar(as.character(labels))) * 0.45)

#' Display text for one or more variable names in a plot title/axis --
#' each variable's current Label if one is set (via the Variables grid, or
#' DEMO_LABELS for a curated demo), else its raw column name. Never used
#' for data lookups (df[[var]] always uses the raw column name -- see
#' apply_metadata()'s note on why columns are never renamed to Label);
#' this only swaps the text a human reads on a chart. `labels` is a
#' name -> label lookup built once in server.R from metadata() and passed
#' into every plot_*() call below; NULL (e.g. a direct Rscript call with
#' no Shiny session) falls back to the raw name unchanged.
var_label <- function(vars, labels = NULL) {
  if (is.null(labels)) return(vars)
  lab <- unname(labels[vars])
  ifelse(is.na(lab) | !nzchar(lab), vars, lab)
}

#' Small "n = ..." caption under a plot, drawn in the outer margin so it
#' doesn't crowd the axis title. Called after the main plotting command.
plot_n_caption <- function(n) mtext(sprintf("n = %d", n), side = 1, line = 2.6, cex = 0.75, col = "#595959", adj = 1)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Descriptive statistics
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#' Mean/median/SD describe a quantity; a nominal or unordered categorical
#' column doesn't have one, "the average blood group" is not a meaningful
#' statistic. Branches on type: scale gets the usual summary, nominal/
#' ordinal get a frequency distribution (counts and percentages) instead --
#' never mean/median/mode/SD forced onto categories.
#'
#' `type` is the Variables grid's declared measurement level ("nominal"/
#' "ordinal"/"scale"), not just is.numeric(x) -- a numeric-coded ordinal
#' column (e.g. education_level 1-4) is kept numeric by apply_metadata()
#' specifically so Spearman/Cronbach/EFA still work on it, so is.numeric()
#' alone can't tell it apart from a scale column. type NULL (a direct call
#' with no Shiny session, e.g. from Rscript) falls back to is.numeric(),
#' matching this function's behaviour before type-awareness was added.
#' Within the categorical branch, ordinal keeps its natural/coded order
#' (table() on a numeric-coded column is already ascending; nothing here
#' re-sorts it), nominal is shown frequency-sorted (Pareto-style, the
#' standard jamovi Frequencies view) since it has no inherent order to
#' preserve -- order is a property of the declared measurement level, not
#' of what the sorted-by-count table happens to look like.
#'
#' `single` (single variable, not batched with others) gets a wide
#' Category/n/% table -- each category's name appears once, not twice
#' (previously "Cash (n)"/"Cash (%)", repetitive at every row). A batched
#' pick (2+ variables run together via combine_batch()) keeps the older
#' statistic/value long shape instead: do.call(rbind, ...) across variables
#' requires identical columns, and a scale variable's summary in the same
#' batch is still statistic/value, so the two shapes can't be mixed.
run_descriptive <- function(df, var, type = NULL, single = TRUE) {
  x_all <- df[[var]]
  is_scale <- if (!is.null(type)) type == "scale" else is.numeric(x_all)
  if (is_scale) {
    x <- x_all[!is.na(x_all)]
    main <- data.frame(
      statistic = c("n", "missing", "mean", "median", "sd", "variance",
                     "min", "max", "range", "iqr", "se"),
      value = c(length(x), sum(is.na(x_all)), round(mean(x), 3),
                round(median(x), 3), round(sd(x), 3), round(var(x), 3),
                round(min(x), 3), round(max(x), 3), round(max(x) - min(x), 3),
                round(IQR(x), 3), round(sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)), 3))
    )
    return(list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = NULL, note = NULL,
                code = sprintf("summary(dat$%s); sd(dat$%s)", var, var)))
  }
  x <- x_all[!is.na(x_all)]
  tab <- table(x)
  if (is.null(type) || type != "ordinal") tab <- sort(tab, decreasing = TRUE)
  pct <- round(100 * prop.table(tab), 1)
  n_note <- sprintf("n = %d, %d missing. Nominal or ordinal data: shown as a frequency distribution (counts and percentages), mean/median/SD do not apply to categories.",
                     length(x), sum(is.na(x_all)))
  if (single) {
    main <- setNames(data.frame(names(tab), as.vector(tab), as.vector(pct), stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
                      c("Category", "n", "%"))
    return(list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = NULL, note = n_note,
                code = sprintf("table(dat$%s)", var)))
  }
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("n", "missing", as.vector(rbind(paste0(names(tab), " (n)"), paste0(names(tab), " (%)")))),
    value = c(length(x), sum(is.na(x_all)), as.vector(rbind(as.vector(tab), as.vector(pct))))
  )
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = NULL,
       note = "Nominal or ordinal data: shown as a frequency distribution (counts and percentages), mean/median/SD do not apply to categories.",
       code = sprintf("table(dat$%s)", var))
}

#' `type`/`single` mirror run_descriptive() above -- same reasons (type
#' tells scale from numeric-coded ordinal, is.numeric() alone can't;
#' single controls whether a scale variable also gets a side-by-side
#' boxplot). The boxplot is deliberately only added when single: nesting
#' its own par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) inside plot_batch()'s *outer* mfrow grid
#' for a multi-variable pick would silently drop every variable's plot but
#' the last (confirmed directly, see the z-score plot's own note on this
#' -- same failure mode, so scale only gets the 2-panel view when it's the
#' only variable being plotted, exactly when plot_batch() calls straight
#' through with no outer grid of its own).
plot_descriptive <- function(df, var, labels = NULL, type = NULL, single = TRUE) {
  x_all <- df[[var]]
  lv <- var_label(var, labels)
  is_scale <- if (!is.null(type)) type == "scale" else is.numeric(x_all)
  if (is_scale) {
    x <- x_all[!is.na(x_all)]
    title <- wrap_title(sprintf("Distribution of %s", lv), width = if (single) 34 else 22)
    if (single) {
      op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), family = "sans")
      on.exit(par(op))
      par(mar = c(4, 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
      hist(x, main = title, xlab = lv, col = "#808080", border = "#ffffff")
      par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
      boxplot(x, main = "Boxplot", ylab = lv, col = "#808080", border = "#333333")
      plot_n_caption(length(x))
    } else {
      plot_theme(); par(mar = c(4, 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
      hist(x, main = title, xlab = lv, col = "#808080", border = "#ffffff")
      plot_n_caption(length(x))
    }
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  x <- x_all[!is.na(x_all)]
  tab <- table(x)
  if (is.null(type) || type != "ordinal") tab <- sort(tab, decreasing = TRUE)
  title <- wrap_title(sprintf("Frequency of %s", lv))
  op <- par(mar = c(rotated_bottom_margin(names(tab)), 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
  on.exit(par(op))
  barplot(tab, main = title, col = "#808080", border = "#ffffff", ylab = "Count", las = 2)
  plot_n_caption(length(x))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Distribution shape
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_distribution <- function(df, var) {
  x <- df[[var]]; x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x); m <- mean(x); s <- sd(x)
  skew <- (sum((x - m)^3) / n) / (s^3)
  se_skew <- sqrt(6 / n)
  z_skew <- skew / se_skew
  p_skew <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_skew)))
  sw <- shapiro.test(x)
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("skewness", "se of skewness", "z (skewness)", "p (skewness test)",
                   "Shapiro-Wilk W", "Shapiro-Wilk p"),
    value = c(round(skew, 3), round(se_skew, 3), round(z_skew, 3), round(p_skew, 4),
              round(unname(sw$statistic), 4), round(sw$p.value, 4))
  )
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = NULL,
       note = ifelse(sw$p.value < 0.05,
                      "p < .05: this variable departs from a normal distribution.",
                      "p >= .05: this variable is consistent with a normal distribution."),
       code = sprintf("shapiro.test(dat$%s)", var))
}

plot_distribution <- function(df, var, labels = NULL) {
  # Histogram with a fitted normal curve overlaid -- the standard way to
  # *see* skew (kept single-panel, not paired with a Q-Q plot, so this
  # composes cleanly inside plot_batch()'s multi-variable grid).
  x <- df[[var]]; x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  lv <- var_label(var, labels)
  title <- wrap_title(sprintf("%s: histogram with fitted normal curve", lv))
  plot_theme(); par(mar = c(4, 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
  m <- mean(x); s <- sd(x)
  h <- hist(x, plot = FALSE)
  curve_x <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 200)
  curve_y <- dnorm(curve_x, m, s)
  ylim <- range(0, h$density, curve_y)
  hist(x, freq = FALSE, main = title, xlab = lv, ylab = "density",
       col = "#808080", border = "#ffffff", ylim = ylim)
  lines(curve_x, curve_y, col = "#333333", lwd = 2)
  plot_n_caption(length(x))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Z-scores and the empirical rule
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Deliberately single-variable only (never routed through plot_batch()):
# plot_zscore() sets its own par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) for the histogram+boxplot
# pair, and plot_batch() sets an *outer* par(mfrow) for however many
# variables are batched -- confirmed directly that nesting the two silently
# drops every variable's plot but the last (PNG has no pages to fall back
# on the way a PDF device does). Distribution shape stays single-panel and
# batchable for the same reason; this technique stays single-variable so it
# can safely be two panels.

run_zscore <- function(df, var) {
  x <- df[[var]]; x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x); m <- mean(x); s <- sd(x)
  z <- (x - m) / s
  within1 <- mean(abs(z) <= 1) * 100
  within2 <- mean(abs(z) <= 2) * 100
  within3 <- mean(abs(z) <= 3) * 100
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("n", "mean", "sd",
                   "% within 1 SD (empirical rule expects ~68%)",
                   "% within 2 SD (empirical rule expects ~95%)",
                   "% within 3 SD (empirical rule expects ~99.7%)",
                   "observations with |z| > 2"),
    value = c(n, round(m, 3), round(s, 3), round(within1, 1), round(within2, 1),
              round(within3, 1), sum(abs(z) > 2))
  )
  idx <- which.max(abs(z))
  fit_note <- if (within2 < 90 || within2 > 99)
    "The empirical rule assumes a normal distribution; this variable's spread departs from that expectation."
  else "This variable's spread is broadly consistent with the empirical rule for a normal distribution."
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = NULL,
       note = sprintf("%s Largest deviation: row %d (value = %s, z = %.2f).",
                       fit_note, idx, format(x[idx]), z[idx]),
       code = sprintf("z <- scale(dat$%s)[, 1]; mean(abs(z) <= 1); mean(abs(z) <= 2); mean(abs(z) <= 3)", var))
}

plot_zscore <- function(df, var, labels = NULL) {
  x <- df[[var]]; x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  lv <- var_label(var, labels)
  m <- mean(x); s <- sd(x)
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), family = "sans")
  on.exit(par(op))
  hist(x, main = "SD bands", xlab = lv, col = "#808080", border = "#ffffff")
  abline(v = m, col = "#000000", lwd = 2)
  for (k in 1:3) {
    abline(v = m + k * s, col = "#595959", lty = 2)
    abline(v = m - k * s, col = "#595959", lty = 2)
  }
  boxplot(x, main = "Boxplot", ylab = lv, col = "#808080", border = "#333333")
  plot_n_caption(length(x))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One-sample tests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_onesample <- function(df, var, mu, test = "ttest") {
  x <- df[[var]]; x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  fn <- if (test == "wilcoxon") wilcox.test else t.test
  res <- fn(x, mu = mu)
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("test statistic", "p-value", "sample mean", "hypothesised value (mu)"),
    value = c(round(unname(res$statistic), 4), round(res$p.value, 4),
              round(mean(x), 3), mu)
  )
  assumptions <- if (test == "ttest") shapiro_row(x) else NULL
  effect_size <- NULL
  if (test == "ttest") {
    d <- (mean(x) - mu) / sd(x)
    ci <- if (!is.null(res$conf.int)) round(res$conf.int, 4) else c(NA, NA)
    effect_size <- data.frame(
      measure = c("Cohen's d", "95% CI (mean)"),
      value = c(sprintf("%.3f (%s)", d, cohend_label(d)),
                sprintf("[%s, %s]", ci[1], ci[2]))
    )
  }
  list(main = main, assumptions = assumptions, effect_size = effect_size, note = NULL,
       code = if (test == "wilcoxon") sprintf("wilcox.test(dat$%s, mu = %s)", var, mu)
              else sprintf("t.test(dat$%s, mu = %s)", var, mu))
}

plot_onesample <- function(df, var, mu, labels = NULL) {
  x <- df[[var]]; x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  lv <- var_label(var, labels)
  title <- wrap_title(sprintf("%s vs test value (mu = %s)", lv, mu))
  plot_theme(); par(mar = c(4, 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
  hist(x, main = title, xlab = lv, col = "#808080", border = "#ffffff")
  abline(v = mu, col = "#333333", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  plot_n_caption(length(x))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two-sample tests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_twosample <- function(df, var, group, test = "ttest", paired = FALSE) {
  form <- as.formula(paste(var, "~", group))
  g <- split(df[[var]], df[[group]])
  if (length(g) != 2) stop("This test needs exactly two groups.")
  if (paired && length(g[[1]]) != length(g[[2]])) stop("A paired test needs equal-length, matched groups.")
  is_nonparam <- test == "mannwhitney"
  # t.test's/wilcox.test's formula methods have never supported paired =
  # TRUE (R has no way to know which row in one group corresponds to which
  # row in the other from a formula alone) -- paired needs the two-vector
  # form, and relies on row order within each group already lining up the
  # same subjects. This is also where "Mann-Whitney U" and "paired
  # Wilcoxon signed-rank" diverge despite both calling wilcox.test(): the
  # same function computes a genuinely different statistic depending on
  # paired=, not just a labelling difference.
  if (paired) {
    res <- if (is_nonparam) wilcox.test(g[[1]], g[[2]], paired = TRUE) else t.test(g[[1]], g[[2]], paired = TRUE)
  } else {
    res <- if (is_nonparam) wilcox.test(form, data = df) else t.test(form, data = df)
  }
  fn_name <- if (is_nonparam) "wilcox.test" else "t.test"
  grp_means <- vapply(g, mean, numeric(1), na.rm = TRUE)
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("test statistic", "p-value", names(grp_means)),
    value = c(round(unname(res$statistic), 4), round(res$p.value, 4),
              round(unname(grp_means), 3))
  )
  assumptions <- NULL
  effect_size <- NULL
  if (!is_nonparam) {
    ci <- if (!is.null(res$conf.int)) round(res$conf.int, 4) else c(NA, NA)
    if (paired) {
      # Paired Cohen's d uses the SD of the differences, not the pooled SD
      # of two independent samples -- a different, smaller-n, correlated
      # design, the independent-samples formula would be the wrong
      # statistic here even though it would run without error.
      diff <- g[[1]] - g[[2]]
      assumptions <- shapiro_row(diff, "Shapiro-Wilk on differences")
      d <- mean(diff, na.rm = TRUE) / sd(diff, na.rm = TRUE)
    } else {
      lv <- levene_test(df[[var]], df[[group]])
      sw <- shapiro_row(df[[var]])
      assumptions <- rbind(lv, sw)
      n1 <- length(g[[1]]); n2 <- length(g[[2]])
      pooled_sd <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * var(g[[1]], na.rm = TRUE) + (n2 - 1) * var(g[[2]], na.rm = TRUE)) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
      d <- (mean(g[[1]], na.rm = TRUE) - mean(g[[2]], na.rm = TRUE)) / pooled_sd
    }
    effect_size <- data.frame(
      measure = c("Cohen's d", "95% CI (mean difference)"),
      value = c(sprintf("%.3f (%s)", d, cohend_label(d)),
                sprintf("[%s, %s]", ci[1], ci[2]))
    )
  }
  list(main = main, assumptions = assumptions, effect_size = effect_size, note = NULL,
       code = if (paired) sprintf("%s(dat$%s[dat$%s == \"%s\"], dat$%s[dat$%s == \"%s\"], paired = TRUE)",
                                   fn_name, var, group, names(g)[1], var, group, names(g)[2])
              else sprintf("%s(%s ~ %s, data = dat)", fn_name, var, group))
}

plot_twosample <- function(df, var, group, labels = NULL) {
  lv <- var_label(var, labels); lg <- var_label(group, labels)
  title <- wrap_title(sprintf("%s by %s", lv, lg))
  plot_theme(); par(mar = c(4, 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
  boxplot(as.formula(paste(var, "~", group)), data = df,
          main = title,
          col = "#808080", border = "#333333", xlab = lg, ylab = lv)
  plot_n_caption(sum(!is.na(df[[var]])))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One-way ANOVA
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_oneway <- function(df, var, group) {
  form <- as.formula(paste(var, "~", group))
  fit <- aov(form, data = df)
  s <- summary(fit)[[1]]
  main <- data.frame(
    term = rownames(s),
    df = s[, "Df"],
    sum_sq = round(s[, "Sum Sq"], 3),
    mean_sq = round(s[, "Mean Sq"], 3),
    f_value = round(s[, "F value"], 4),
    p_value = round(s[, "Pr(>F)"], 4)
  )
  tukey <- TukeyHSD(fit)[[1]]
  tukey_df <- data.frame(
    comparison = rownames(tukey),
    diff = round(tukey[, "diff"], 3),
    lwr = round(tukey[, "lwr"], 3),
    upr = round(tukey[, "upr"], 3),
    p_adj = round(tukey[, "p adj"], 4)
  )
  ss_between <- s[1, "Sum Sq"]; ss_within <- s[2, "Sum Sq"]
  eta_sq <- ss_between / (ss_between + ss_within)
  assumptions <- rbind(levene_test(df[[var]], df[[group]]),
                        shapiro_row(residuals(fit), "Shapiro-Wilk on residuals"))
  effect_size <- data.frame(measure = "Eta-squared", value = round(eta_sq, 4))
  list(main = main, assumptions = assumptions, effect_size = effect_size,
       note = "See the Tukey HSD table (in R code output) for which specific group pairs differ.",
       code = sprintf("aov(%s ~ %s, data = dat); TukeyHSD(fit)", var, group))
}

plot_oneway <- function(df, var, group, labels = NULL) {
  lv <- var_label(var, labels); lg <- var_label(group, labels)
  title <- wrap_title(sprintf("%s by %s (diamonds mark group means)", lv, lg))
  plot_theme(); par(mar = c(4, 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
  boxplot(as.formula(paste(var, "~", group)), data = df,
          main = title,
          col = "#808080", border = "#333333", xlab = lg, ylab = lv)
  means <- tapply(df[[var]], df[[group]], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  points(seq_along(means), means, pch = 18, col = "#000000", cex = 1.6)
  plot_n_caption(sum(!is.na(df[[var]])))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Kruskal-Wallis (non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_kruskal <- function(df, var, group) {
  form <- as.formula(paste(var, "~", group))
  res <- kruskal.test(form, data = df)
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("chi-squared", "df", "p-value"),
    value = c(round(unname(res$statistic), 4), unname(res$parameter),
              round(res$p.value, 4))
  )
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = NULL, note = NULL,
       code = sprintf("kruskal.test(%s ~ %s, data = dat)", var, group))
}

run_correlation <- function(df, x, y, method = "pearson") {
  res <- cor.test(df[[x]], df[[y]], method = method)
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("correlation coefficient", "test statistic", "p-value"),
    value = c(round(unname(res$estimate), 4), round(unname(res$statistic), 4),
              round(res$p.value, 4))
  )
  effect_size <- NULL
  r <- unname(res$estimate)
  mag <- if (abs(r) < 0.1) "negligible" else if (abs(r) < 0.3) "weak"
         else if (abs(r) < 0.5) "moderate" else "strong"
  if (method == "pearson" && !is.null(res$conf.int)) {
    ci <- round(res$conf.int, 4)
    effect_size <- data.frame(
      measure = c("Magnitude", "95% CI (r)"),
      value = c(mag, sprintf("[%s, %s]", ci[1], ci[2]))
    )
  } else {
    effect_size <- data.frame(measure = "Magnitude", value = mag)
  }
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = effect_size,
       note = "Correlation describes association, not causation.",
       code = sprintf("cor.test(dat$%s, dat$%s, method = \"%s\")", x, y, method))
}

#' All pairwise correlations among 3+ variables in one table, the
#' JASP/jamovi "correlation matrix" view rather than one pair at a time.
#' Pairwise p-values via a manual cor.test() loop, not Hmisc::rcorr(), to
#' avoid a new package dependency for one convenience function.
run_correlation_matrix <- function(df, vars, method = "pearson") {
  if (length(vars) < 2) stop("Pick at least two variables for a correlation matrix.")
  mat <- df[, vars, drop = FALSE]
  pairs <- utils::combn(vars, 2)
  rows <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs)), function(k) {
    v1 <- pairs[1, k]; v2 <- pairs[2, k]
    ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(mat[[v1]], mat[[v2]], method = method))
    data.frame(var1 = v1, var2 = v2, r = round(unname(ct$estimate), 4), p_value = round(ct$p.value, 4))
  })
  main <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = NULL,
       note = "Correlation describes association, not causation.",
       code = sprintf("cor(dat[, c(%s)], method = \"%s\", use = \"pairwise.complete.obs\")",
                       paste(sprintf('"%s"', vars), collapse = ", "), method))
}

plot_correlation_matrix <- function(df, vars, method = "pearson", labels = NULL) {
  mat <- df[, vars, drop = FALSE]
  lvars <- var_label(vars, labels)

  n <- length(vars)

  # Wider left AND bottom margin than plot_theme()'s default: both axes'
  # labels are full column names (or longer display labels) at las = 2
  # (rotated), not the short default axis text the standard margin was
  # sized for -- clipped otherwise (same rotated_bottom_margin() fix as
  # the other las = 2 barplots below).
  op <- par(mar = c(rotated_bottom_margin(lvars), max(6, max(nchar(lvars)) * 0.5), 3, 1))

# Chi-squared
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_chisquare <- function(df, cat1, type = "goodness", cat2 = NULL) {
  if (type == "fisher") {
    # Fisher's exact test: the safer alternative to chi-squared association
    # specifically when expected cell counts are too small for the
    # chi-squared approximation to be trusted (base R fisher.test(), no new
    # dependency -- confirmed working directly on the same table structure
    # chisq.test() already uses here).
    if (is.null(cat2) || !nzchar(cat2)) stop("Fisher's exact test needs a second categorical variable.")
    tab <- table(df[[cat1]], df[[cat2]])
    res <- fisher.test(tab)
    main <- data.frame(statistic = "p-value", value = round(res$p.value, 4))
    effect_size <- NULL
    if (!is.null(res$estimate)) {
      ci <- if (!is.null(res$conf.int)) round(res$conf.int, 4) else c(NA, NA)
      effect_size <- data.frame(
        measure = c("Odds ratio", "95% CI (odds ratio)"),
        value = c(round(unname(res$estimate), 4), sprintf("[%s, %s]", ci[1], ci[2]))
      )
    }
    return(list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = effect_size,
                note = "Fisher's exact test does not rely on the chi-squared approximation, the safer choice when expected cell counts are small.",
                code = sprintf("fisher.test(table(dat$%s, dat$%s))", cat1, cat2)))
  }
  if (type == "association" && !is.null(cat2) && nzchar(cat2)) {
    tab <- table(df[[cat1]], df[[cat2]])
    res <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
    n <- sum(tab)
    v <- cramers_v(res$statistic, n, nrow(tab), ncol(tab))
    low_expected <- any(res$expected < 5)
    code <- sprintf("chisq.test(table(dat$%s, dat$%s))", cat1, cat2)
  } else {
    tab <- table(df[[cat1]])
    res <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
    n <- sum(tab)
    v <- cramers_v(res$statistic, n, length(tab), 2)
    low_expected <- any(res$expected < 5)
    code <- sprintf("chisq.test(table(dat$%s))", cat1)
  }
  main <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("chi-squared", "df", "p-value"),
    value = c(round(unname(res$statistic), 4), unname(res$parameter), round(res$p.value, 4))
  )
  effect_size <- data.frame(measure = "Cramer's V", value = round(v, 4))
  note <- if (low_expected) "Warning: at least one expected cell count is below 5; the chi-squared approximation may be unreliable. Consider Fisher's exact test instead." else NULL
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = effect_size, note = note, code = code)
}

plot_chisquare <- function(df, cat1, type = "goodness", cat2 = NULL, labels = NULL) {
  lc1 <- var_label(cat1, labels)
  plot_theme()
  if ((type == "association" || type == "fisher") && !is.null(cat2) && nzchar(cat2)) {
    lc2 <- var_label(cat2, labels)
    tab <- table(df[[cat1]], df[[cat2]])
    obs <- as.vector(tab)
    exp <- as.vector(suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))$expected)
    labs <- outer(rownames(tab), colnames(tab), paste, sep = "\n")
    lab_vec <- as.vector(t(labs))
    title <- wrap_title(sprintf("%s by %s: observed vs expected", lc1, lc2))
    op <- par(mar = c(rotated_bottom_margin(unlist(strsplit(lab_vec, "\n"))), 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
    on.exit(par(op))
    bp <- barplot(rbind(obs, exp), beside = TRUE, names.arg = lab_vec,
                  main = title,
                  col = c("#595959", "#bfbfbf"), las = 2, cex.names = 0.7,
                  legend.text = c("Observed", "Expected"))
  } else {
    tab <- table(df[[cat1]])
    exp <- rep(sum(tab) / length(tab), length(tab))
    title <- wrap_title(sprintf("%s: observed vs expected", lc1))
    par(mar = c(4, 4, title_top_margin(title), 1))
    barplot(rbind(as.vector(tab), exp), beside = TRUE, names.arg = names(tab),
            main = title,
            col = c("#595959", "#bfbfbf"), legend.text = c("Observed", "Expected"))
  }
}

run_reliability <- function(df, items) {
  item_df <- df[, items, drop = FALSE]
  res <- cronbach_alpha(item_df)
  item_total <- sapply(items, function(nm) {
    other <- rowSums(item_df[, setdiff(items, nm), drop = FALSE])
    round(cor(item_df[[nm]], other, use = "complete.obs"), 3)
  })
  main <- data.frame(statistic = "Cronbach's alpha", value = round(res$alpha, 4))
  effect_size <- data.frame(item = items, item_total_correlation = unname(item_total))
  label <- if (res$alpha >= 0.9) "excellent" else if (res$alpha >= 0.8) "good"
           else if (res$alpha >= 0.7) "acceptable" else if (res$alpha >= 0.6) "questionable"
           else "poor"
  list(main = main, assumptions = NULL, effect_size = effect_size,
       note = sprintf("Alpha = %.3f: %s internal consistency for this %d-item set.", res$alpha, label, res$k),
       code = sprintf("items <- dat[, c(%s)]\n# alpha <- (k/(k-1)) * (1 - sum(item variances) / var(total score))",
                       paste(sprintf('"%s"', items), collapse = ", ")))
}

# Exploratory factor analysis
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_factoranalysis <- function(df, items, factors = 2, rotation = "varimax") {
  item_df <- df[, items, drop = FALSE]
  # Suitability checks (is this data worth factor-analysing at all?), not
  # dependent on factanal() converging, so computed even when it fails.
  kmo <- tryCatch(kmo_measure(item_df), error = function(e) NULL)
  bart <- tryCatch(bartlett_sphericity(item_df), error = function(e) NULL)
  assumptions <- NULL
  if (!is.null(kmo) && !is.null(bart)) {
    kmo_label <- if (kmo$overall >= 0.8) "good" else if (kmo$overall >= 0.6) "acceptable" else "poor"
    assumptions <- data.frame(
      check = c("Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (overall)", "Bartlett's test of sphericity"),
      statistic = c(round(kmo$overall, 4), round(bart$chi_sq, 4)),
      df = c(NA, bart$df),
      p_value = c(NA, round(bart$p_value, 4)),
      result = c(sprintf("%s sampling adequacy for factor analysis", kmo_label),
                 ifelse(bart$p_value < 0.05, "Correlations are large enough for factor analysis (p < .05)",
                        "Correlations may be too small for factor analysis (p >= .05)"))
    )
  }
  fit <- tryCatch(
    factanal(item_df, factors = factors, rotation = rotation),
    error = function(e) e
  )
  if (inherits(fit, "error")) {
    return(list(main = data.frame(message = "Factor analysis could not run."),
                assumptions = assumptions, effect_size = NULL,
                note = paste("R reported:", conditionMessage(fit),
                              "-- try fewer factors or more items."),
                code = sprintf("factanal(dat[, c(%s)], factors = %d, rotation = \"%s\")",
                                paste(sprintf('"%s"', items), collapse = ", "), factors, rotation)))
  }
  load_mat <- unclass(fit$loadings)
  main <- data.frame(item = rownames(load_mat), round(load_mat, 3), row.names = NULL)
  effect_size <- data.frame(item = items, uniqueness = round(fit$uniquenesses, 3))
  pval <- if (!is.null(fit$PVAL)) round(fit$PVAL, 4) else NA
  list(main = main, assumptions = assumptions, effect_size = effect_size,
       note = if (!is.na(pval)) sprintf("Goodness-of-fit test p-value: %s (small p suggests more factors may be needed).", pval) else NULL,
       code = sprintf("factanal(dat[, c(%s)], factors = %d, rotation = \"%s\")",
                       paste(sprintf('"%s"', items), collapse = ", "), factors, rotation))
}

plot_factoranalysis <- function(df, items, factors = 2, rotation = "varimax", labels = NULL) {
  item_df <- df[, items, drop = FALSE]
  fit <- tryCatch(factanal(item_df, factors = factors, rotation = rotation), error = function(e) NULL)
  plot_theme()
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    plot.new(); text(0.5, 0.5, "Factor analysis did not converge.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  load_mat <- unclass(fit$loadings)
  litems <- var_label(rownames(load_mat), labels)
  op <- par(mar = c(rotated_bottom_margin(litems), 4, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(op))
  barplot(t(load_mat), beside = TRUE, names.arg = litems,
          main = sprintf("Factor loadings (%d factors)", factors),
          col = c("#333333", "#595959", "#8c8c8c", "#bfbfbf")[seq_len(ncol(load_mat))],
          legend.text = colnames(load_mat), las = 2, ylab = "Loading")
}

#' Heuristic column typing: non-numeric -> nominal; numeric with <= 7 distinct
#' whole-number values -> ordinal (overridable by the user); else scale.
detect_types <- function(df) {
  is_id_like <- function(name) grepl("(^id$|_id$)", trimws(name), ignore.case = TRUE)
  types <- vapply(names(df), function(nm) {
    col <- df[[nm]]
    if (!is.numeric(col)) return("nominal")
    u <- unique(col[!is.na(col)])
    if (length(u) <= 7 && all(u == round(u))) "ordinal" else "scale"
  }, character(1))
  # A column literally named "id"/"...id" is almost always a row identifier,
  # not a measurement -- excluded from analysis by default (Drop = TRUE),
  # not just retyped, so it doesn't clutter grouping-variable pickers either.
  # Users can un-drop it via the Variables grid if a given column genuinely
  # is meant as data (rare).
  drop <- is_id_like(names(df))
  data.frame(
    Name = names(df), Type = unname(types), Label = "",
    Missing = "", ValueLabels = "", Drop = drop,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

  kv <- strsplit(pairs, "=")
  vals <- vapply(kv, function(p) trimws(p[1]), character(1))
  labs <- vapply(kv, function(p) trimws(p[2]), character(1))
  stats::setNames(labs, vals)
}

#' Apply the metadata grid (type, missing codes, value labels, drop, rename to
#' label) to a raw data.frame. Returns the analysis-ready data.frame. Never
#' mutates the raw/original data held elsewhere -- caller keeps that separate.
apply_metadata <- function(df, meta) {
  keep <- meta$Name[!meta$Drop]
  df <- df[, intersect(names(df), keep), drop = FALSE]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(meta))) {
    nm <- meta$Name[i]
    if (!nm %in% names(df)) next
    codes <- parse_codes(meta$Missing[i])
    if (length(codes) > 0) df[[nm]][as.character(df[[nm]]) %in% codes] <- NA
    # Value-label recoding happens BEFORE the type branch below, and only
    # for nominal columns: recoding to text and then immediately forcing
    # as.numeric() back on an ordinal column would turn every value NA
    # (as.numeric("High School") is NA) -- a real bug this caught, not a
    # hypothetical one. Ordinal columns keep their numeric codes; document
    # what the codes mean in Label instead (e.g. "Education level, 1-4").
    if (meta$Type[i] == "nominal") {
      vl <- parse_value_labels(meta$ValueLabels[i])
      if (!is.null(vl)) {
        recoded <- unname(vl[as.character(df[[nm]])])
        df[[nm]] <- ifelse(is.na(recoded), as.character(df[[nm]]), recoded)
      }
      df[[nm]] <- factor(df[[nm]])
    } else {
      # Ordinal stays numeric (e.g. Likert 1-5 codes) so it can still feed
      # Spearman correlation, Cronbach's alpha, and factor analysis --
      # matching how the module itself treats ordinal items (see
      # variable_type_guide.csv: "median, frequencies, and Spearman").
      # "Ordinal" is a measurement-level tag for which tests get offered,
      # not a change of storage type, so ValueLabels is not applied here.
      df[[nm]] <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[nm]]))
    }
  }
  # Deliberately NOT renaming columns to their Label here. Every run_*()
  # builds formulas via as.formula(paste(var, "~", group)) with no
  # backtick-quoting for non-syntactic names -- a Label containing spaces
  # or punctuation (e.g. "Education level (1=High School, ...)") would
  # silently break formula parsing or column lookups the moment a real
  # label existed (caught live: picker choices carry the raw Name as their
  # value via named_choices() in server.R, so working_data() must keep raw
  # Names too, or v <- input$var_numeric no longer resolves against df).
  # Label is display-only: the Variables grid and the Analyse picker
  # already show it (named_choices()); results/plots show the raw column
  # name, matching what a reproducible R script would actually use.
  df
}

#' Apply a stack of filters (list of list(var, op, val)) as AND conditions.
apply_filters <- function(df, filters) {
  for (f in filters) {
    if (!f$var %in% names(df)) next
    col <- df[[f$var]]
    keep <- switch(f$op,
      "=" = as.character(col) == f$val,
      "!=" = as.character(col) != f$val,
      ">" = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(col)) > suppressWarnings(as.numeric(f$val)),
      "<" = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(col)) < suppressWarnings(as.numeric(f$val)),
      "contains" = grepl(f$val, as.character(col), fixed = TRUE),
      rep(TRUE, nrow(df))
    )
    keep[is.na(keep)] <- FALSE
    df <- df[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  df
}

#' 1.5x IQR outlier flag for one numeric column, returns a logical vector.
outlier_flags <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- q[2] - q[1]
  x < (q[1] - 1.5 * iqr) | x > (q[2] + 1.5 * iqr)
}

#' Build variable-picker choices as a named vector (display Label -> raw
#' column Name) so every picker shows the same friendly text as the
#' Variables grid, not the raw snake_case column name -- the picker is the
#' other place a missing label was actually visible to a user, seeding
#' Label alone on the Data tab wasn't enough.
named_choices <- function(names_vec, meta) {
  if (length(names_vec) == 0) return(character(0))
  labels <- meta$Label[match(names_vec, meta$Name)]
  display <- ifelse(!is.na(labels) & nzchar(labels), labels, names_vec)
  stats::setNames(names_vec, display)
}

#' Build a table's HTML as a plain string: APA-style (top rule, header
#' underline, bottom rule, no vertical lines, numeric columns right-aligned,
#' optional caption above). Single source of truth for both the on-screen
#' card (via renderTable_html(), wrapped in HTML()) and the standalone HTML
#' export file, so the two never drift apart.
#'
#' A batch result (combine_batch(), several variables run through the same
#' technique) carries a "variable" column repeating the same value down
#' every row for that variable -- correct data, but a poor table: the
#' variable name belongs in a heading above each variable's own block, not
#' repeated as a column value on every single row. Detected and split here,
#' once, so every caller (on-screen results, HTML export) gets this for
#' free rather than needing the same special-casing at each call site.
table_to_html <- function(df, caption = NULL) {
  if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) return("")
  if ("variable" %in% names(df)) {
    groups <- unique(df$variable)
    parts <- vapply(groups, function(v) {
      sub <- df[df$variable == v, setdiff(names(df), "variable"), drop = FALSE]
      table_to_html(sub, caption = v)
    }, character(1))
    return(paste(parts, collapse = ""))
  }
  numeric_col <- vapply(df, is.numeric, logical(1))
  esc <- function(x) htmltools::htmlEscape(as.character(x))
  thead <- paste0("<tr>", paste0("<th>", esc(names(df)), "</th>", collapse = ""), "</tr>")
  rows <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(df)), function(i) {
    cells <- vapply(seq_along(df), function(j) {
      cls <- if (numeric_col[j]) " class=\"num\"" else ""
      sprintf("<td%s>%s</td>", cls, esc(df[i, j]))
    }, character(1))
    paste0("<tr>", paste(cells, collapse = ""), "</tr>")
  }, character(1))
  cap <- if (!is.null(caption)) sprintf('<p class="table-caption">%s</p>', esc(caption)) else ""
  sprintf('%s<div class="result-table-wrap"><table class="result-table"><thead>%s</thead><tbody>%s</tbody></table></div>',
          cap, thead, paste(rows, collapse = ""))
}

#' Render a data.frame as the app's existing HTML table styling (no reliance
#' on Shiny's tableOutput widget, so it matches the ported CSS exactly).
renderTable_html <- function(df, caption = NULL) {
  if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) return(NULL)
  htmltools::HTML(table_to_html(df, caption))
}

#' Combine a list of per-variable run_*() results (same shape) into one,
#' prefixing each table with a "variable" column. This is the batch-analysis
#' mechanism: descriptive, distribution, one-sample, two-sample, one-way
#' ANOVA, and Kruskal-Wallis all accept more than one numeric variable and
#' run the same technique on each, returning one combined table, the same
#' pattern JASP/jamovi's Descriptives and T-Tests modules use.
combine_batch <- function(vars, results) {
  add_var_col <- function(d, v) {
    if (is.null(d)) return(NULL)
    cbind(variable = v, d, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }
  stack <- function(field) {
    parts <- Map(add_var_col, lapply(results, `[[`, field), vars)
    parts <- Filter(Negate(is.null), parts)
    if (length(parts) == 0) return(NULL)
    do.call(rbind, parts)
  }
  notes <- Filter(Negate(is.null), Map(function(v, r)
    if (!is.null(r$note)) sprintf("%s: %s", v, r$note) else NULL, vars, results))
  list(
    main = stack("main"),
    assumptions = stack("assumptions"),
    effect_size = stack("effect_size"),
    note = if (length(notes) == 0) NULL else paste(unlist(notes), collapse = " "),
    code = paste(vapply(results, function(r) r$code, character(1)), collapse = "\n")
  )
}

#' Render several single-variable plot_*() calls into one multi-panel plot.
plot_batch <- function(vars, plot_fn_single) {
  n <- length(vars)
  if (n <= 1) { plot_fn_single(vars[1]); return(invisible(NULL)) }
  ncols <- ceiling(sqrt(n)); nrows <- ceiling(n / ncols)
  op <- par(mfrow = c(nrows, ncols))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (v in vars) plot_fn_single(v)
}

#' Render a base-R plotting function to a PNG data URI, so a plot can sit
#' inside a renderUI-driven card without a plotOutput/session binding.
plot_to_datauri <- function(plot_fn) {
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
  grDevices::png(tmp, width = 900, height = 620, res = 130)
  tryCatch(plot_fn(), finally = grDevices::dev.off())
  raw <- readBin(tmp, "raw", file.info(tmp)$size)
  unlink(tmp)
  paste0("data:image/png;base64,", base64enc::base64encode(raw))
}

#' Build a real, APA-style draft interpretation sentence from a technique's
#' actual computed result (never a fixed template with fabricated numbers)
#' -- a starting point for the write-up box the student edits into their
#' own words, not a submitted answer. Returns NULL for categories with no
#' template defined (batched descriptive/distribution mixes of variables
#' don't reduce to one sentence the same way a single test does).
build_report_paragraph <- function(category, result) {
  get_stat <- function(main, name) {
    row <- which(main$statistic == name)
    if (length(row) == 0) return(NA)
    main$value[row[1]]
  }
  get_eff <- function(effect_size, name) {
    if (is.null(effect_size)) return(NA)
    row <- which(effect_size$measure == name)
    if (length(row) == 0) return(NA)
    effect_size$value[row[1]]
  }
  fmt_p <- function(p) {
    p <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(p))
    if (is.na(p)) "NA" else if (p < .001) "< .001" else sprintf("= %.3f", p)
  }
  sig_word <- function(p, yes = "a statistically significant", no = "no statistically significant") {
    p <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(p))
    if (is.na(p)) "an inconclusive" else if (p < .05) yes else no
  }

  switch(category,
    onesample = {
      m <- result$main
      t <- get_stat(m, "test statistic"); p <- get_stat(m, "p-value")
      mean_v <- get_stat(m, "sample mean"); mu <- get_stat(m, "hypothesised value (mu)")
      sprintf("A one-sample test found %s difference from the benchmark value of %s (sample mean = %s, test statistic = %s, p %s).",
              sig_word(p), mu, mean_v, t, fmt_p(p))
    },
    twosample = {
      t <- get_stat(result$main, "test statistic"); p <- get_stat(result$main, "p-value")
      d <- get_eff(result$effect_size, "Cohen's d")
      extra <- if (!is.na(d)) sprintf(", Cohen's d = %s", d) else ""
      sprintf("The comparison found %s difference between the two groups (test statistic = %s, p %s%s).",
              sig_word(p), t, fmt_p(p), extra)
    },
    oneway = {
      m <- result$main
      row <- which(m$term != "Residuals")[1]
      f <- m$f_value[row]; p <- m$p_value[row]
      eta <- get_eff(result$effect_size, "Eta-squared")
      sprintf("The one-way ANOVA found %s difference among the groups (F = %s, p %s%s).",
              sig_word(p), f, fmt_p(p), if (!is.na(eta)) sprintf(", eta-squared = %s", eta) else "")
    },
    kruskal = {
      chi <- get_stat(result$main, "chi-squared"); p <- get_stat(result$main, "p-value")
      sprintf("The Kruskal-Wallis test found %s difference among the groups (chi-squared = %s, p %s).",
              sig_word(p), chi, fmt_p(p))
    },
    correlation = {
      r <- get_stat(result$main, "correlation coefficient"); p <- get_stat(result$main, "p-value")
      mag <- get_eff(result$effect_size, "Magnitude")
      sprintf("There was %s%s relationship (r = %s, p %s). Correlation describes association, not causation.",
              sig_word(p), if (!is.na(mag)) paste0(" ", mag) else "", r, fmt_p(p))
    },
    chisquare = {
      chi <- get_stat(result$main, "chi-squared"); p <- get_stat(result$main, "p-value")
      v <- get_eff(result$effect_size, "Cramer's V")
      sprintf("The chi-squared test found %s pattern (chi-squared = %s, p %s%s).",
              sig_word(p), chi, fmt_p(p), if (!is.na(v)) sprintf(", Cramer's V = %s", v) else "")
    },
    regression = {
      m <- result$main
      row <- which(m$term != "(Intercept)")[1]
      est <- m$estimate[row]; p <- m$p_value[row]
      r2 <- get_eff(result$effect_size, "R-squared")
      sprintf("The regression found %s relationship (coefficient = %s, p %s, R-squared = %s). A good prediction is still not proof of causation.",
              sig_word(p), est, fmt_p(p), r2)
    },
    NULL
  )
}

#' Build a complete, self-contained HTML report for one result entry: the

#' exactly), the plot embedded as a base64 PNG, assumptions/effect size,
